MOLECULAR CYTOGENETICS LABORATORY REPORT
[redacted location] Children's Hospital
Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine

PATIENT INFORMATION
Patient: [redacted name]
MRN: [redacted ID]
DOB: [redacted date]
Age: 6 years
Specimen Type: Fresh tissue biopsy
Specimen Site: Right thigh mass
Date Collected: [redacted date]
Date Received: [redacted date]
Date Reported: [redacted date]

CLINICAL HISTORY
This 6-year-old patient presents with an enlarging right thigh mass. Laboratory evaluation reveals elevated creatine kinase levels. Clinical suspicion for alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma.

TEST PERFORMED
Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization (FISH) Analysis
Probe: Dual-color FOXO1 break-apart probe (13q14.11)
Catalog: Vysis LSI FOXO1 Dual Color Break Apart Rearrangement Probe

METHODOLOGY
FISH analysis was performed on touch preparations from fresh tissue using a dual-color break-apart probe for the FOXO1 gene locus at 13q14.11. The probe consists of a 5' green fluorescent probe and a 3' red fluorescent probe flanking the FOXO1 breakpoint region. In normal cells, the green and red signals appear fused or in close proximity. A rearrangement is indicated by separation of the red and green signals.

RESULTS
FOXO1 GENE REARRANGEMENT: POSITIVE

Quantitative Analysis:
- Total cells analyzed: 200
- Cells with FOXO1 rearrangement: 156
- Percentage positive: 78%
- Normal signal pattern (2 fusion signals): 44 cells (22%)
- Rearranged signal pattern (1 fusion, 1 red, 1 green): 156 cells (78%)

The established laboratory cutoff for a positive result is >10% of cells showing split signals.

INTERPRETATION
The detection of FOXO1 gene rearrangement in 78% of analyzed cells confirms the diagnosis of alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (ARMS). This rearrangement typically results from a translocation creating a fusion gene between FOXO1 (previously known as FKHR) and either PAX3 (t(2;13)(q35;q14)) or PAX7 (t(1;13)(p36;q14)). These fusion proteins function as aberrant transcription factors with enhanced transcriptional activity compared to wild-type PAX proteins.

The PAX3-FOXO1 fusion occurs in approximately 55% of ARMS cases, while PAX7-FOXO1 accounts for approximately 22%. The remaining cases may harbor variant translocations or be fusion-negative. The presence of a FOXO1 rearrangement is associated with a more aggressive clinical course and poorer prognosis compared to embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma.

CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
The molecular confirmation of FOXO1 rearrangement has important therapeutic implications:

1. Risk Stratification: FOXO1-positive ARMS is classified as high-risk disease regardless of other clinical factors
2. Treatment Intensity: Requires intensive multimodal therapy per high-risk rhabdomyosarcoma protocols
3. Prognostic Significance: Associated with higher rates of metastasis and relapse

RECOMMENDATIONS
1. Initiate intensive systemic chemotherapy according to high-risk rhabdomyosarcoma protocols (e.g., VAC/VI regimen with vincristine, actinomycin D, cyclophosphamide alternating with vincristine and irinotecan)
2. Plan for aggressive local control measures including surgical resection when feasible and/or radiation therapy
3. Consider maintenance therapy following initial treatment
4. Close monitoring for metastatic disease with appropriate imaging studies
5. Molecular testing of the primary tumor to identify the specific fusion partner (PAX3 vs PAX7) may provide additional prognostic information
6. Consider enrollment in clinical trials for FOXO1-positive rhabdomyosarcoma if available

Reported by: [redacted name], PhD, FACMG
Reviewed by: [redacted name], MD, PhD
Board Certified in Clinical Cytogenetics and Molecular Genetic Pathology
